claim: hk4165692682 estimated division_jaccard ~0.22 by a paired-submission ablation: LB 0.929 with divisions on, 0.907 with the division-creating step off, so 0.022 = 0.1 x div_jaccard.
quote: normal: LB 0.929 divisions off: LB 0.907 difference 0.022 = 0.1 × division_jaccard so my division_jaccard ≈ 0.22

claim: Two competitors on the same 0.948 LB can need opposite work: div_j 0.30 requires edge 0.918, div_j 0.15 requires edge 0.933, and the leaderboard hides which.
quote: if your division_jaccard is 0.30, you only need adj_edge_jaccard 0.918 if it is 0.15, you need adj_edge_jaccard 0.933 Those two people should be working on opposite things, and the leaderboard shows them the same number.

claim: The 0.22 paired-LB estimate is confounded: dropping a division also drops a daughter edge, so the 0.022 delta splits between the edge and division terms and 0.22 is a bound, not a measurement.
quote: if turning off division creation means your linker only keeps one of the two daughter links instead of two, the dropped daughter becomes an edge false negative, not just a division miss. That would pull edge_jaccard down as well

claim: A nearest-parent candidate graph at R~9.9um K<=10 covers only ~88% of the 151 GT division forks versus ~99.7% of continuation edges, a hard ceiling on division_jaccard before any classifier runs.
quote: a simple nearest-parent candidate graph (R≈9.9µm, K≤10) only reaches ~88% coverage on the 151 GT division forks, versus ~99.7% on plain continuation edges — so there's a real, measurable gap concentrated on divisions before any classifier even gets involved

claim: One competitor's ILP never exceeded division_jaccard 0.0004 at any division weight; at weight 0.5 it found div_tp=1 alongside 3260 false forks, so weight-tuning alone cannot produce a positive division score.
quote: For me division_jaccard never rises above 0.0004, at any weight tested. Even at 0.5, where the ILP does find 1 real division (div_tp=1), it does so alongside 3260 false ones. div_j = tp/(tp+fp+fn) ≈ 1/3260 - swamped to near-zero by the FP volume.

claim: A Hungarian 1:1 linker with divisions bolted on afterwards as a hand-written distance+image rule reaches divJ ~0.12.
quote: my linker is basically 1:1 right now. hungarian assignment frame to frame. then i add divisions in a totally separate step after on top of the result. so the division decision never actually sees the model. its js a hand written rule with distance and image checks. my divJ is around 0.12

claim: A third self-report of division_jaccard around 0.2, given only approximately.
quote: I don't know how I did in edge division but I think its something like 0.2

claim: Immediately after the July patch, adjusted_edge_jaccard plateaued at ~0.90-0.91 across public approaches and division_jaccard was ~0 for essentially everyone.
quote: adjusted_edge_jaccard plateaus around ~0.90–0.91 — the field is on the same split_0 stack, and the post-proc knobs (disappearance cost, D4/9-way TTA, gap-closing) seem to top out there. division_jaccard ≈ 0 for essentially everyone under the patch.

claim: Detection is not the division ceiling: on 7 labelled divisions the parent and both daughters were detected 7/7 within the 7um radius, yet both parent->daughter edges were present 0/7 and predicted parent out-degree was 1 every time.
quote: parent and both daughters detected 7/7 (100%) both parent->daughter edges in my graph 0/7 exactly one edge present 7/7 predicted parent out-degree 1, every single time

claim: hengck23: bright thin lines visible at frame t are the signature of a division that occurred a few frames EARLIER, making the strongest division cue retrospective rather than at the split frame.
quote: typo: bright thin lines at time t are new cell divisions that happen before t (maybe a few frames before). It is very good clue to detect division

claim: hengck23 could not get good division results from appearance alone and is looking for another signal, after manually inspecting crop series along trajectories.
quote: My first instinct is to find the upper bound of achievable division Jaccard. I would use the human correct rate as a proxy or oracle. From my observations, just by appearance above alone, i don't get good results. I need to think of something else.

claim: The acquisition frame rate is too coarse to see a cell slowly split: a division appears as a cell suddenly becoming two objects already far apart, which is why continuous-deformation cues fail.
quote: the frame rate seems to be too large for us to observe the slow splitting of a cell. It is like the cell "suddenly becomes two (and far apart)"

claim: hengck23's only reliable human cue for a division is exclusion from context: confidence in the neighbouring tracks, since the parent cannot simply disappear - implying divisions are only recoverable where surrounding links are already high-confidence.
quote: i can only be very sure it is a division when the neighbour track is very obvious, so that since the parent cell cannot disappear, it must be split. This means that IPL can only make a correct division only if the neighbour tracks has very high confidence?

claim: Even for a human, a division can be hard to distinguish from a false positive link: hengck23 describes a division as looking like two different crop series concatenated together.
quote: For division, I can sometimes see 2 "different series being concatenated together". In fact, it may be difficult for humans to tell if it is FP or division?

claim: Measured on 8 labelled parents and 299 ordinary nodes from 5 films: peak intensity separates divisions at AUC 0.73 at the split frame (0.68-0.70 for daughters t+1..t+3), local contrast 0.55-0.69, and elongation is at chance (0.34-0.58).
quote: Peak intensity separates them at AUC 0.73 for the parent at t, then 0.68, 0.70, 0.70 for t+1 to t+3. Local contrast 0.55, 0.65, 0.69, 0.64. An intensity weighted elongation measure does not separate at all: 0.34, 0.48, 0.58, 0.56, which is chance.

claim: Labelled divisions do NOT cluster in time within a film: across 25 films with labelled divisions, division times spread by a median of 32 frames out of 100 - evidence against hengck23's 'find one and you find many' synchrony claim, on the labelled subset.
quote: Synchrony, labels only: 25 films have labelled divisions, 8 have two or more. Within one film the labelled division times spread by a median of 32 frames (8 to 38) out of 100. So the labelled divisions do not cluster.

claim: Motion statistics calibrated on the real lineage edges: 1.86 um/frame median step, +0.30 lag-1 directional persistence, 7.24 um sister separation - the persistence term is a multi-frame signal available before any fork is proposed.
source: topic 732103 post 3507381 by José Freitas Alves Neto
quote: Motion is calibrated on the real lineage edges: 1.86 µm/frame median step, +0.30 lag-1 directional persistence, 7.24 µm sister separation.

claim: Broken continuations sit at the same separation as real sister pairs (orphan median 8.5-10 um vs 7.24 um calibrated sister separation), so no distance gate can separate daughters from linker failures - the decision must use appearance, motion history, or better localisation.
quote: Jose calibrated sister separation at 7.24 um from the real lineage edges; my orphan median is 8.5-10 um. A distance gate cannot separate the two populations. Whatever decides daughter-vs-broken-track has to use something else

claim: Both Ultrack zebrafish reference configs use max_distance 10.0 and max_neighbors 5 with small balanced event penalties (division 0.001 or 0.1), whereas the public Kaggle lineage fork sets division 1.2 / disappearance 1.5 / appearance 0, under which a fork can never be optimal.
quote: Both zebrafish configs in the supplementary repo use max_distance 10.0 and max_neighbors 5, and the event penalties are small and balanced: large_zebrafish has appear 0.002, disappear 0.001, division 0.001; sparse_zebrafish has all three at 0.1.

claim: In the public Kaggle lineage pipeline the division penalty is set so high relative to disappearance that a fork can never be the optimal solution of the objective.
quote: The public lineage I forked runs division at 1.2 and disappearance at 1.5 with appearance at 0. I had already worked out on my own solver's objective that a fork can never be optimal at those values

claim: An asymmetric gate is needed: allowing out-degree 2 is necessary but not sufficient, because a continuation-tuned distance gate rejects the second arc before capacity is consulted; the second arc needs roughly double the first arc's radius.
quote: Allowing out-degree 2 was necessary and not sufficient, because a gate tuned for continuations rejects the second arc before capacity ever gets consulted. What the numbers say is that the second arc needs a different gate from the first: tight for a continuation

claim: Measured reachability of both division arcs versus gate radius on 7 labelled divisions: 2/7 inside 7.0 um, 5/7 inside 9.9 um, 6/7 inside 12.0 um, 7/7 inside 15.0 um (predicted-node positions, so detector error is included).
quote: both steps inside a 7.0 um gate 2/7 (29%) both steps inside a 9.9 um gate 5/7 (71%) both steps inside a 12.0 um gate 6/7 (86%) both steps inside a 15.0 um gate 7/7 (100%)

claim: Argument for solving divisions inside the optimisation rather than post hoc: a wide gate inside a competitive objective is only used where the non-division explanation is worse, whereas a post-hoc gate is global and every widening buys false positives everywhere.
quote: If division and non-division hypotheses compete inside one optimisation, the wide gate only gets used where the alternative explanation is worse, so you do not pay for it everywhere. Doing it afterwards, the way my pipeline does, the gate is global and every widening buys false positives

claim: hengck23's planned division design is late-stage tracklet association, not per-frame fork proposal: get detection and tracking right first, assume birth/death only at the image boundary, then infer splits from long tracks with tracklets as nodes.
quote: my current strategy is to have good cell detection and tracking. Then infer division from long track ( stage 3 ). I assume death/birth can only happen at image boundary, so maybe we can detect splits from long tracks, ie i treat division as tracklet association problem, tracklet as node association

claim: The tracklet-association framing tested negative: the interior-orphan pool is ~400x larger than the events it should contain (1,289 interior orphans on four films holding 3 labelled divisions).
quote: Those four films hold 3 labelled divisions; the whole train set holds 151 across 87 of the 199 label files. So the pool is roughly 400x larger than the events it is meant to contain.

claim: In the public 0.938 pipeline family the motion-relink stage rebuilds the edge list from a one-to-one Hungarian assignment before safe-div runs, destroying every fork the ILP produced - so any upstream division work is invisible.
quote: In the public 0.938 pipeline family the motion-relink stage rebuilds the edge list from a one-to-one Hungarian assignment before safe-div runs, so every fork the ILP produced is destroyed there. If you inherit that post-processing, any division work upstream of it is invisible.

claim: A Hungarian one-to-one linker forfeits the entire division term by construction - no node can have two outgoing edges, so division_jaccard is exactly 0.000 (40 FN of 40 in the test), leaving 0.1 of the available 1.1 unreachable.
quote: A Hungarian linker forfeits the whole division term by construction. One successor per cell means no node ever has two outgoing edges, so division Jaccard is exactly 0.000 — in my test, 40 FN out of 40 — and 0.1 of the available 1.1 is gone before the tracker sees an image.

claim: The host's own HOCT (general_v0) division-aware tracker, fed synthetic ball masks from point detections, over-linked, produced spurious forks rather than recovering real divisions, and ran ~45 min/movie - not submission-viable.
quote: On my train movies it under-performed a tuned ILP on the edge term (it over-links), produced spurious forks rather than recovering real divisions, and ran ~45 min/movie on the open-source solver — so it's not submission-viable as-is with this input.

claim: hengck23's proposed route to a division detector: inspect ROI crops t-10..t+10 around Kaggle parent nodes in napari to confirm the appearance signature, then hand-label with focus3d's human-in-the-loop click annotation and train a detector on those labels.
quote: it is not difficult to use focus3d framework to hand-label these because it supports human-in-the-loop annotation (basically click a point like SAM). then you can train a division detector

claim: hengck23 asserts many real divisions are not annotated in the Kaggle ground truth, and that they are not hard to identify because divisions rarely occur singly.
quote: i think many cell divisions are not annotated in the Kaggle data. It is not so difficult to identify them (and i think when you find one, you are likely to find many others. it is rare only one cell splits).

claim: hengck23 warns that because the annotation is sparse, an apparently long parent-to-daughter step may be recorded as a short one, biasing any geometry measured on labels.
quote: note that the annotation is sparse. it is possible that the "long parent" is annotated short.

claim: The labels cover track SEGMENTS, not whole lineages: of 572 labelled tracks, 351 begin after frame 0 and 391 end before the last frame, median length 35 frames - so the 36/151 labelled divisions are a biased subset, not an unbiased sample of all divisions.
quote: Of 572 labelled tracks, 351 begin after frame 0 and 391 end before the last frame, median length 35 frames, while all 25,733 labelled edges span exactly one timepoint. So the 36 divisions are a labelled subset, not an unbiased sample of every division in the movies.

claim: Only ~2.8% of nuclei are annotated in the training ground truth and there are ~304 division events across all 199 videos - a count roughly double the 151 fork figure others report, suggesting the two counts differ by the parent-vs-daughter unit.
source: topic 732103 post 3507381 by José Freitas Alves Neto
quote: The training ground truth is sparse — roughly 2.8% of nuclei are annotated, and across all 199 videos there are about 304 division events.

claim: The real GT division rate is ~0.26% of nodes counted as mitotic parents; the synthetic set inflates it to 4.07%, a 15.7x ratio for positive-class reweighting.
source: topic 732103 post 3521156 by José Freitas Alves Neto
quote: the 4.07% figure is in that same unit — mitotic parents divided by all nodes, i.e. 165,267 / 4,056,226. So it's directly comparable to the ~0.26% real rate I quoted; both are "fraction of nodes that are a dividing parent."

claim: The 0.91-0.94 real-nuclei detectability reference comes from sparse annotations and annotators tend to label unambiguous cells, so that reference is probably optimistic - direct support for annotation selection bias toward easy cases.
source: topic 732103 post 3521156 by José Freitas Alves Neto
quote: the 0.91–0.94 real reference comes from the sparse annotations (~2.8% of nuclei), and annotators tend to label unambiguous cells — so that reference is probably optimistic, and I haven't measured how real recall varies with density.

claim: The real training set comes from only 2 actual embryos, which differ enormously: annotation sparsity ~1% vs ~9% and division counts 26 vs 125 across their samples.
quote: our real training set turns out to come from only 2 actual embryos, and they differ a lot annotation sparsity of roughly 1% vs 9%, and division counts of 26 vs 125 across their samples.

claim: The ground truth follows only ~22 tracks per movie rather than every cell, so an unannotated blob is not a missed detection - the metric never sees unlabelled cells as edge false positives.
quote: The ground truth follows ~22 tracks per movie, not every cell, but 100% of its edges span exactly one frame — no gap-closing to learn, and an unannotated blob is not a missed detection.

claim: The patched division metric requires genuine strongly-connected parent->two-daughter structure matched within a 7 um distance radius; forks that do not match a real GT division register as false positives.
quote: The patch (now public in the repo) requires divisions to be genuine strongly-connected parent→two-daughter structures matched within the 7 µm distance radius. The far-away synthetic forks now register as false positives instead of true positives

claim: Pre-patch the division match relied on weakly-connected-component structure and did not require a fork to sit near a real GT division, which is what the hub-node exploit abused to push division_jaccard from ~0 to ~1.0.
quote: In the pre-patch version, that matching relied on weakly-connected-component structure and did not strictly require each matched division to be a genuine parent→two-daughter fork sitting near a real GT division.

claim: The host confirmed a division-Jaccard metric exploit, published a patch in royerlab/kaggle-cell-tracking-competition, and re-scored all submissions; non-exploiting submissions were unaffected.
quote: A few of you might be aware that an exploit of our metrics was found, specifically in the division Jaccard score. We have made a patch and will re-score all submissions as soon as possible (likely Monday). Submissions that did not actively exploit this will not have their scores affected.

claim: The 17 July patch (commit aa65e90) closed three holes at once: divisions now need directed local topology instead of shared weak connectivity, edges spanning more than one frame are dropped, and merged edges are collapsed; pre-July local CV numbers are not comparable.
quote: The metric was patched on 17 July (commit aa65e90), closing three holes at once: divisions now require directed local topology rather than shared weak connectivity, edges spanning more than one frame are dropped, and merged edges are collapsed.

claim: Measured on the same graphs, the hub-and-fake-fork exploit moved a 1:1 linker 0.9839 -> 1.0639 under the old metric but 0.9839 -> 0.9794 under the patched one, i.e. it now loses score.
quote: appending a hub node and 40 fake forks moved a one-to-one linker 0.9839 → 1.0639 under the old metric and 0.9839 → 0.9794 under the new one

claim: Over-detection is nearly free under the metric (a predicted node matching no GT node is never a false positive; the line is exactly 1 - 0.1 x over-prediction), so detection recall is worth far more than precision.
quote: A predicted node that matches no ground-truth node is never a false positive; the whole cost is the adjusted-Jaccard term. The line is exactly 1 − 0.1 × over-prediction, so 10% more nodes has to buy only a 1% relative gain in edge Jaccard to break even.

claim: Duplicate detections cost ~9% and buy nothing: node matching is one-to-one bipartite, so a twin one voxel away matches nothing and only inflates the node count - taking a union of two models' detections without a merge pass pays this in full.
quote: Duplicating a detection costs ~9% and buys nothing. Node matching is a one-to-one bipartite assignment, so a twin one voxel away matches nothing: edge Jaccard did not move at all, only the node count.

claim: Counter-argument to prioritising divisions: post-patch the top was 0.914-0.929 while division_jaccard was ~0 for essentially everyone, so the observed frontier separation came from the edge term, not divisions.
quote: Yet the post-patch top is 0.914–0.929, so the separation comes from somewhere. For those above ~0.914 — not asking for methods — is your gain on the edge term (a genuinely better/retrained model pushing adj_edge past ~0.91), or on divisions

claim: Hypothesis that the two score terms are not independent: a cleaner edge model would let the ILP form divisions natively, with divisions riding on long-range link recall rather than needing a dedicated division effort.
quote: My hunch is that a cleaner edge model would let the ILP form divisions natively (divisions riding on long-range link recall) — i.e. the two terms aren't independent.

claim: Base rate against divisions: 151 divisions across all 199 training movies, one link in 853, and 112 of the 199 movies contain none at all.
quote: Divisions: 151 in total, i.e. one link in 853, and 112 of the 199 movies contain none at all.

claim: The dominant bottleneck on division score is argued to be the rare-event base rate - a few hundred events among hundreds of thousands of nodes - rather than model architecture.
quote: it suggests the rare-event nature of divisions (a few hundred events among hundreds of thousands of annotated nodes) is probably the dominant bottleneck for most people's division score, more than model architecture per se

claim: Weight-tuning offers only two bad options - suppress everything for div_j=0, or let a few real forks through buried under thousands of false ones with div_j still ~0 - so no meaningful positive division score is reachable that way.
quote: It can only choose between "suppress everything, div_j=0" (weight 1.0) or "let a few real ones through, buried under thousands of fake ones, div_j still ≈0" (weight 0.5–0.65). Neither path gets me a meaningful positive division score.

claim: Missed divisions are not random: they concentrate in crowded frames with ~3x the node count and closer neighbours, and each failure trips 2-3 checks at once, so loosening any single threshold recovers nothing and only adds false positives.
quote: theyre almost all in crowded frames. like 3x the node count of the ones i get right and closer neighbours. and when i checked why each one failed basically none of them fail for js one reason. they fail 2 or 3 checks at once. so loosening any single threshold recovers nothing

claim: The public Ultrack zebrafish_embryo.ome.zarr reports voxel scale 1.625 x 0.40625 x 0.40625 um and shape (522, 1, 505, 2217, 2170), matching the Kaggle voxel size exactly - so the Ultrack paper's sparse-zebrafish Fig.6 dataset is the same acquisition family as the competition data.

A free CC0 synthetic dataset provides 165,267 labelled mitotic-parent divisions across 4,056,226 nodes (~540x the competition's mitosis supervision), generated by a physical model with the evaluator's exact stride-4 XY downsampling.
source: topic 732103 post 3507381 by José Freitas Alves Neto
quote: 165,267 labelled divisions across 4,056,226 nodes That is roughly 540× more mitosis supervision than the competition ground truth provides.

claim: In the synthetic dataset both daughters inherit the parent's track_id, so nodes[:,4] is a lineage/clone id rather than a unique track - building a candidate graph off track_id makes cells appear to teleport.
source: topic 732103 post 3521156 by José Freitas Alves Neto
quote: both daughters inherit the parent's track_id. So nodes[:, 4] is a lineage/clone id, not a unique track — after a division, two distinct tracks share it. The unambiguous lineage lives in edges (and a node with two outgoing edges is exactly a mitosis).

claim: CRITICAL: support/division_metrics.py on disk is the PRE-PATCH (exploitable) division scorer using weak connectivity; the current patched scorer is reference/royerlab-baseline/src/tracking_cellmot/division_metrics.py, which uses _is_strongly_connected_division. Tuning against support/ calibrates to the closed exploit.
quote: support/: 'All matched prediction nodes in a single weakly-connected component of the prediction graph.'  reference/: 'Merely sharing a weakly connected component is not sufficient.'

claim: A predicted fork that matches no GT node, is not a local candidate at any GT division window, and has matched evidence on at most one child branch is scored as NEITHER TP NOR FP - it is completely free under the patched metric.
quote: Otherwise, unmatched, structurally valid forks with no local GT evidence are ignored.

claim: The free-fork rule is confirmed by the baseline's own unit test: a fork whose parent is unmatched and where only one of two branches has matched GT evidence yields DivisionCounts(tp=0, fn=0, fp=0).
quote: """One branch with no matched child or grandchild provides no evidence.""" ... assert evaluate_divisions(pred, gt, max_distance=1.0) == DivisionCounts(tp=0, fn=0, fp=0,)

claim: Exactly four things make a predicted fork a division FALSE POSITIVE: (a) the fork node itself matches an annotated GT node with out-degree>=1; (b) it was a local candidate at a GT division window but failed topology or lost the bipartite pairing; (c) two distinct child branches have nearest matched evidence in different GT weakly-connected components; (d) its local branches merge.
quote: fp_forks = (considered | evaluable_forks | invalid_forks) - tp_forks

claim: Only forks landing on ANNOTATED GT nodes are 'evaluable' as FPs: the fork must match a GT node within 7 um whose GT node still has an outgoing edge. With ~2.8% of nuclei annotated, the great majority of speculative forks never enter the FP tally at all.
quote: evaluable_forks = {pred_id for pred_id in pred_forks if pred_id in pred_to_gt and gt_graph.out_degree(pred_to_gt[pred_id]) >= 1}

claim: A fork on a matched GT node whose annotation ENDS there (out-degree 0) is deliberately excluded from the FP tally, because the scorer cannot tell whether the cell really divided - so forking at the end of an annotated segment is also free.
quote: A matched GT node with no children marks the end of the annotation - we can't tell whether the cell actually divided there, so such predicted divisions are excluded from the count (and therefore from the FP tally).

claim: The most dangerous fork is the one that bridges two different annotated GT tracks: if two direct-child branches have nearest matched evidence in distinct GT weakly-connected components the fork is an unconditional FP, matched or not.
quote: for pred_id in pred_forks: ... else: if len(set(branch_evidence)) >= 2: cross_component_forks.add(pred_id)

claim: Near-misses at real divisions are penalised where distant speculation is not: any fork sitting on a matched parent-side node of a GT division window (or its immediate successor) enters 'considered' and becomes an FP if it fails the topology test or loses the pairing.
quote: local_nodes = parent_ids | {successor for parent_id in parent_ids for successor in matched_pred.successors(parent_id)} local_forks = local_nodes & pred_div_nodes considered |= local_forks

claim: The division matching window is exactly four timepoints: grandparent -> dividing parent -> children -> grandchildren, extracted per GT division; predicted nodes are matched independently against that window at 7 um, so the fork may be one frame early or late.
quote:
grandparent -> dividing parent -> children -> grandchildren
```
This window permits a predicted fork one timepoint before or after the GT split without using graph-wide reachability.

claim: The TP topology test is local and directed: the fork must be, or be the immediate successor of, a node matched to the GT divider or its predecessor, and the fork's two child-lineages ({child} u successors(child)) must cover two distinct GT daughter lineages under a bipartite matching.
quote: pred_parent_ids = {pred_div, *pred_graph.predecessors(pred_div)} if pred_parent_ids.isdisjoint(parent_ids): return False

claim: Daughter evidence may arrive at different timepoints and a grandchild can stand in for an unmatched direct child, so a division can still score TP when only one daughter is detected at t+1 and the other only at t+2.
quote: A bipartite matching must associate the two GT daughter lineages with two different predicted branches. The two supporting matches may occur at different timepoints within the window.

claim: A fork is rejected as malformed if a child used by the fork has any other parent, or if a fallback grandchild is shared - so merge-then-split structures cannot score and are charged as FPs.
quote: A direct child used by the fork must have that fork as its sole parent. When grandchild fallback is needed, each grandchild must belong to that child alone. A locally merged or shared branch is rejected.

claim: division_jaccard is micro-averaged: TP/FP/FN are summed across every video in the split before the Jaccard is taken, so a handful of FPs on one movie dilutes TPs won on another; and if no divisions exist anywhere the term is dropped entirely.
quote: has_divisions = (div_tp + div_fp + div_fn) > 0 division_jaccard = _jaccard(div_tp, div_fp, div_fn) if has_divisions else float("nan")

claim: One predicted fork can be credited to at most one GT division and one GT division to at most one fork (maximum-cardinality bipartite pairing), which is what closed the hub-node exploit - so duplicating forks around a real division buys nothing and costs FPs.
quote: A maximum-cardinality bipartite matching is then computed so each pred fork serves at most one GT division, and each GT division is paired with at most one pred fork.

claim: Predicted nodes that match no GT node are never edge false positives either - the sparse ground truth makes over-detection structurally cheap, penalised only through the adjusted-Jaccard node-count term with a=0.1.
quote: Because the ground truth is sparse, a correct prediction will inevitably include nodes and edges the ground truth doesn't cover. Predicted nodes that do not match a ground-truth node are not counted as false positives.
